title: Cytoreduction plus low‐dose aspirin versus cytoreduction alone as primary prophylaxis of thrombosis in patients with high‐risk essential thrombocythaemia: an observational study

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:p>The effectiveness of low‐dose aspirin in the primary prevention of thrombosis in patients with high‐risk essential thrombocythaemia (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ET</jats:styled-content>) treated with cytoreductive drugs is not well established. The risk‐benefit balance of low‐dose aspirin plus cytoreductive therapy compared with cytoreduction alone was retrospectively analysed in 247 patients with high‐risk <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ET</jats:styled-content> without prior thrombosis. Follow‐up was 763 and 685 person‐years for cytoreduction plus low‐dose aspirin and cytoreduction alone, respectively. The rate of thrombosis was not significantly reduced in patients on cytoreduction plus aspirin (14·4 events per 1000 person‐years) when compared with those on cytoreduction alone (24·8 events per 1000 person‐years; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0·2). However, in the subgroup of patients older than 60 years, the addition of low‐dose aspirin was associated with a significantly lower rate of thrombosis (8·6 vs. 29·2 thrombosis per 1000 person‐years for combined treatment and cytoreduction alone, respectively, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0·02). The rate of major bleeding was significantly higher with combined therapy than with cytoreduction alone both in the whole series (14·4 vs. 1·4 haemorrhagic events per 1000 person‐years, respectively, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0·006) and in the subgroup of patients older than 60 years. In conclusion, low‐dose aspirin benefits high‐risk <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ET</jats:styled-content> patients older than 60 years receiving cytoreductive therapy as primary prophylaxis of thrombosis.</jats:p>
